title: Ecological Economics
text:
2 Learning Goals
Upon completion of this seminar, you will be able to:
Expertise:

Understand the core concepts and analytical perspective of ecological economics
Explain how different notions of ‘economic development’ relate to the question of ecological sustainability
Discuss the relevance of trade-offs between social and environmental goals
Understand how economic activities and the resulting ecological stressors are globally interrelated

Methodological Competence:

Work with data on socio-economic development and environmental pressures
Account for environmental stressors at the global level, distinguishing production- and consumption-based perspectives
Evaluate environmental policy instruments and their underlying assumptions

Social and Personal Skills:

Conduct and present a country-level analysis as part of a group
Be able to delineate the assumptions on which your own assessments, and those on others depend when it comes to the discussion of social and environmental challenges
Take well-founded positions in current debates (e.g. growth vs. degrowth)

title: Ecological Economics
text:
📑 The course in brief
The course covers a wide range of interactions between the environment and socio-economic development. Students are introduced to various methods for analyzing economic impacts on the environment, the importance of the environment for economic activities, and the role of social institutions within the context of economy–environment relationships. In this setting, students learn about different policy tools that can address (undesired) external effects of economic activities on the environment and how to evaluate the effectiveness of environmental regulations from an economic perspective.
Focus:

Analyze the interactions between the environment and socio-economic development
Learn methods for assessing economic impacts on the environment and the environment’s importance for economic activity
Understand and evaluate environmental policy tools — conventional and non-conventional — from an economic perspective

How:

The course is taught as a seminar with lectures, interactive elements, and group work.
Over the semester, students work on one particular country or region case study, which they present as a poster during a poster conference at the end of the semester (see the examination page).
It is offered jointly for the MA “Sustainable Energy” and the MA “International Management Studies” programs.

Prerequisites:

There are no formal prerequisites. A basic familiarity with introductory economics is helpful.



🎯 Learning Objectives
Expertise:

Understand the core concepts and analytical perspective of ecological economics
Explain how different notions of ‘economic development’ relate to the question of ecological sustainability
Discuss the relevance of trade-offs between social and environmental goals
Understand how economic activities and the resulting ecological stressors are globally interrelated

Methodological Competence:

Work with data on socio-economic development and environmental pressures
Account for environmental stressors at the global level, distinguishing production- and consumption-based perspectives
Evaluate environmental policy instruments and their underlying assumptions

Social and Personal Skills:

Conduct and present a country-level analysis as part of a group
Be able to delineate the assumptions on which your own assessments, and those on others depend when it comes to the discussion of social and environmental challenges
Take well-founded positions in current debates (e.g. growth vs. degrowth)

title: Examination — the country-analysis poster
text: The examination for this course is a poster on a country or region case study, which you prepare in groups and present during the poster conference at the end of the semester.

title: Examination — the country-analysis poster
section: Content and guiding questions for the poster
text:
Content and guiding questions for the poster
Students are expected to prepare a poster (DIN-A0) and to pitch it to the other students during the poster conference at the end of the course (max. 5 minutes per student). Each student will be asked questions about the content they were responsible for. Students will prepare the poster together in groups of up to 3 people.
The goal of the poster is to present an analysis of the main challenges faced by a specific country or region, which students selected during the second week of lectures. Make sure you choose a country or region whose documents are available in a language you understand and from which you can access the necessary data (see the data hints). In their analysis, students are expected to identify key socio-ecological challenges of the country or region, describe and evaluate current solution strategies, and critically discuss these strategies while suggesting improvements.
More precisely, the analysis involves three major steps.
First, students are expected to identify a set of challenges to the country/region, which they consider essential. They need to justify their choice precisely. Challenges can refer to economic, social and/or ecological problems, e.g.:

Excessive reliance on fossil fuels
Extensive externalization of ecological costs into other countries (‘living at the expense of others’) or serving as a sink for ecological problems caused by other countries (being ‘exploited for the sake of others’)
Problems in ensuring a decent level of well-being for the whole population
Relevance of national energy poverty
Excessive levels of income and/or wealth inequalities
Problems in achieving the SDGs
Excessive inflation and political polarization
Problems to remain within planetary boundaries1

It is crucial that you justify why you consider these challenges essential and worth examining. You also need to be clear about your value system, for example, when arguing that the current level of inequality in a country is ‘unjust.’ Students are then expected to explain how the country or region currently addresses the challenges described above and to critically analyze the current strategy.
Here are some brief examples (your own analysis should go into much more detail, of course):

One of the main challenges for France is the excessive reliance on nuclear energy. The current government does not perceive this as a major problem for various reasons. We believe that because of generational justice, water scarcity, and global justice arguments this needs to change. Investment in green energy is required and should be financed by a wealth tax.
One of Bangladesh’s main challenges is the high poverty rate and gender inequality. Currently, the country tries to become more competitive through low prices and environmentally harmful activities. This is problematic; the country should focus on building a green technology industrial base. International development collaboration is necessary.
One of Germany’s main challenges is decarbonizing energy production and consumption. The country aims to diversify its energy sources and strongly supports the development, use, and import of green hydrogen. Consequently, political leaders and German companies are not only promoting domestic green hydrogen production but also importing it from countries mostly in the Global South, such as Chile, Morocco, or Nigeria. This approach risks creating social injustices and resource exploitation similar to colonialism. Therefore, it is important to carefully design these hydrogen partnerships, for example by including sustainability criteria for green hydrogen production in the exporting countries, to ensure socio-economic benefits are created locally.
Morocco has achieved success in developing renewable energy. One challenge in the Moroccan energy transition is dependence on foreign investments and ownership, which creates social injustices due to limited socio-economic opportunities for small actors and a lack of involvement and participation from rural communities. Supportive measures for small actors, such as implementing a feed-in tariff and government support for domestic actors, are necessary.

In the final step, students are asked to suggest ways to improve or even redirect the current strategy. This includes analyzing risks, opportunities, and success factors for the new approach.
For each step, if you have doubts or questions, please ask us for feedback.

title: Examination — the country-analysis poster
text:
Examination
The posters need to be printed individually and brought to the class on the day of the poster presentation. A digital copy of the poster must be uploaded on Moodle one week before your presentation.
The final mark for the course depends on the quality of the students’ poster and their performance during the final poster presentation. The criteria for the evaluation are described below. The following specifics apply to the overall evaluation of the work:

A contribution that is not graded as at least adequate in dimensions #3 (“formalities”), #4 (“clarity and comprehensibility of argument”), #5 (“correctness and accuracy of exposition”) or #8 (“spelling and grammar”) will be graded 5.0.
If the work receives only a sufficient or satisfactory rating in dimensions #4 (“clarity and comprehensibility of argument”) or #5 (“correctness and accuracy of exposition”), the overall rating cannot receive a grade better than ‘sufficient’ (4.0) or ‘satisfactory’ (3.0).
If a student provides a certificate for diagnosed dyslexia before submitting the work, dimension #8 (“spelling and grammar”) will be ignored.

Apart from these special features, the overall rating results from the individual ratings in each assessment dimension. The “Weight” column shows the relative importance of each dimension for the overall score. For each dimension, we use an average reference value; special characteristics of the work may lead to upgrades or downgrades. The overall grade depends on the percentage of maximum points earned. A work that scores the reference value in each dimension receives a grade of 2.7. For the points in section I, only the poster itself is considered. For the final scores in sections II and III, both the poster and the oral presentation are evaluated, with the primary focus on the poster. Section IV considers only the oral performance.
It is very important that when submitting their poster, groups indicate precisely which student was mainly responsible for which part of the final work, or which parts were prepared by all students equally. Depending on how students distribute the work within their group, not all evaluation dimensions might be relevant for each student. In such cases, the corresponding dimensions will simply be ignored when computing the final mark.
